newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU fish chief says "quota hoppers" can be caught.
newsitem.headline: EU fish chief says "quota hoppers" can be caught.

text.p: "Quota hoppers," foreign fishing vessels which register in another country to grab part of the national quota, can be stopped within existing rules, according to European Union Fisheries Commissioner Emma Bonino.
The problem is most acute in Britain, where around 150 foreign, mainly Spanish, vessels are registered and take 20 percent of the national fish quota.
Britain has warned that the situation must be ended before agreement can be reached on proposed sharp cuts in the EU fleet aimed at saving endangered fish stocks.
"I think this problem is not increasing but they (the British) have to live with what they have," Bonino told Reuters in a recent interview.
The combative Italian commissioner said Britain's belated start-up last year of an EU scheme to compensate fishermen for laying up vessels should help stop further quota hoppers.
The scheme had been delayed by the British government's reluctance to provide funds to match EU aid.

"If European fishermen have bought U.K. licences or boats it's because U.K. fishermen have sold," Bonino said in her characteristically blunt style. "They sold because the decommissioning scheme was not available."
Britain wanted a common market but not common rules, she said, adding that Britain did not want fish catches by quota hoppers to be counted against the national quota.
Bonino pointed out that national quotas existed for milk, olive oil and other agricultural products and that fish could not be made an exception.
"If you want to go and buy a piece of land in Tuscany and produce olive oil it will be counted in the Italian quota," she said.
Britain has said that it will demand changes to the EU treaty on fisheries quotas at an ongoing inter-governmental conference.
But Bonino said this would take a long time and would be very difficult as any changes would have to be agreed unanimously.
It would be quicker and easier for the British government to introduce non-discriminatory regulations on fish catch landings and social security to discourage "quota hoppers," she added.

Although British-registered vessels have to visit British ports twice a year, the government has not been prepared to impose fish catch landing measures because this would create problems for Scottish boats fishing in French waters, Bonino said.

Looking ahead to the next EU fisheries ministers meeting on October 14, Bonino said she was optimistic that a framework agreement could be reached on controversial proposals to reduce EU fishing capacity by up to 40 percent over six years.
"I'm confident that we can reach a general conclusion at the council," she said. "No member state contests that there is overcapacity...but each says its up to the neighbour to reduce."
The collapse of North Sea herring fishing this summer showed the cost of mismanagement, she said, adding that member states had watered down proposals for radical quota cuts.
